economics.competition-mcq-class.0001.all: A single firm supplies the whole market

economics.costs-assess-3.0004.all: Raise revenue: raise price (depends on PED - smartphones branded, may be inelastic), increase sales via advertising/new models; cut costs: cheaper suppliers, efficiency, economies of scale, cut staff. Evaluate: price rise may lose customers to rivals; cost cutting may lower quality; depends on competition and which costs rose.

economics.costs-data.0002.b: Fuel up 33% raises variable costs; pay rise raises labour costs; total costs rise, profit (already small) falls, may cut investment/drivers or go into loss; may pass costs on to customers.
economics.costs-data.0002.c: For: maintain margin, all rival delivery firms face same fuel rise so may also raise prices; profit grew 15% 2024-25 though. Against: price elastic demand if competitive market, lose customers; alternatives - cut costs, more efficient routes. Judgement depends on PED, competitors, size of rise.

economics.costs-evaluate-2.0001.all: For: doubles output, lower average fixed cost per unit if demand exists, economies of scale, higher revenue. Against: higher fixed costs £6,000+, risk if demand doesn't double, financing/borrowing costs, maintenance. Judgement: depends on demand, cost of machine, cash flow.

economics.costs-evaluate-3.0003.all: Raise prices (PED), increase sales/marketing, cut costs (suppliers, efficiency, wages), economies of scale; revenue rose 15% but costs faster so focus on cost control. Evaluate trade-offs: quality, competition, PED. Judgement.

economics.costs-mcq-def.0001.all: Costs that do not change when the level of output changes, such as rent

economics.demand-analyse-1.0004.all: Income up 5%: frozen yoghurt normal good -> demand rises (shift right); cheaper own-brand substitute -> demand falls; health campaigns change tastes - may raise (healthier than ice cream) or reduce (sugar) demand; overall net effect depends.

economics.demand-analyse-2.0001.all: More consumers -> demand for local goods shifts right; young families -> more demand for schools, childcare, nappies, housing; new estates -> demand for local shops, transport; age structure changes composition of demand.

economics.demand-define1.0007.all: A good for which demand rises when incomes rise.

economics.demand-define2.0004.all: An increase in quantity demanded (1) caused by a fall in the product's own price - a movement down/along the demand curve (1).

economics.demand-describe.0016.all: More people means more households needing somewhere to live (1), so more buyers/renters at each price, demand curve shifts right (1).

economics.demand-diagram.0005.all: Shift D right to D1; new higher equilibrium price P1 and higher quantity Q1.

economics.demand-explain.0020.all: Fall in price of coffee machines -> extension of demand for machines; complements (coffee pods/capsules, coffee beans) jointly demanded so demand for them increases, shifts right; more owners of machines buy more pods.

economics.demand-mcq-class.0002.all: A rise in the price of petrol

economics.demand-mcq-def.0001.all: The amount of a product that buyers want and can afford to purchase at each price over a period of time

economics.demand-state-class.0003.all: A change in the price of fresh juice

economics.demand-state-id.0007.all: a leftward shift of the demand curve for fizzy drinks

economics.economic-problem-analyse-1.000.all: Limited tax revenue (scarce resources) vs unlimited wants (health, education, roads); must choose/prioritise; opportunity cost - spending on healthcare means less on roads; growing 17m population increases demands; may borrow or raise taxes.

economics.economic-problem-analyse-2.000.all: Scarce skilled labour -> cannot expand output, may pay higher wages raising costs; raw materials up 11% -> higher costs, lower profit or higher prices; may substitute capital/train workers; growth limited.

economics.economic-problem-analyse-3.000.all: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone = full-time job, €376/week income (approx €19.5k/yr), work experience; versus future higher earnings as engineer; also leisure/independence forgone.

economics.economic-problem-define1.0001.all: When there are not enough resources to satisfy unlimited wants.

economics.economic-problem-define2.0005.all: The factor of production that organises the other factors (1) and takes risks to produce goods/services (1).

economics.economic-problem-describe.0004.all: Firms invest in new machinery/factories (1), funded by saving/profits or government subsidies/lower interest rates, adding to the capital stock (1).

economics.demand-diagram.0005.problem: Grammatical error in the stem: 'Butter are a normal good'.
economics.demand-diagram.0005.fix: Change to 'Butter is a normal good.' Mark scheme is otherwise correct.

economics.demand-mcq-def.0001.problem: Option C ('a want for a product that is backed by the ability to pay') is effective demand, which is itself a valid definition of demand, so two options are arguably correct.
economics.demand-mcq-def.0001.fix: Replace C with a clear distractor, e.g. 'The amount of a product that firms are willing and able to supply at each price'.
